newsitem.title: DUBAI: Rising fuel prices a concern at Dubai cargo meet.
newsitem.headline: Rising fuel prices a concern at Dubai cargo meet.

text.p: Rising jet fuel prices and their potential impact in the short term for air cargo costs provide an unplanned backdrop to a four day meeting of the world's airfreight industry starting Sunday, industry sources said.

Delegates at The International Air Cargo Association (TIACA) will also have in mind bullish forecasts for air cargo growth over both the medium and long term, forecasts which are driven by the continued expansion of the Asia-Pacific economies, the globalisation of world production, and the continued rapid development of the express delivery market.

In its outlook to 2015 published in October, Boeing forecasts that air cargo volumes will grow at an annual average of 6.6 percent a year, compared to 5.1 percent for passenger traffic, with the world economy growing at three percent annually.
It also sees the international express market expanding at an 18 percent annual rate to account for 37 percent of the overall market in 20 years, against only five percent in 1995.

McDonnell Douglas in its estimate, also published this month, sees cargo traffic gaining 7.4 percent annually till 2014, with passenger traffic rising at 5.9 percent and puts world economic growth at an annual 3.3 percent over the period.

At the same time, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) has just released the figures from its annual five year outlook for air freight growth, and sees an average growth rate of 6.6 percent a year to 2000. Last year IATA forecast 10.5 percent growth to 1999, but this has been tempered by the downturn since at end-1995 and early 1996.

Air cargo, which represents around a third of world trade by value, is also an important early indicator of a region's or a country's economic performance. Reuter surveys on air cargo business from European airports have shown an improving export outflow since the summer of this year, a trend most noticeable in the case of the UK.

The most recent survey from London on October 16 suggested that ex-UK air cargo is now at its strongest since the start of 1996, with Asian demand leading the way, followed by Latin America and for the first time this year, there has been a significant upturn in westbound volumes across the Atlantic.

Airfreight volumes from Hong Kong, 75 percent or more of whose outward traffic is represented by goods made in China, are also showing a sharp upturn, partly as result of traditional end-year seasonal demand, but also due to an improving economic performance by its key markets such as North America, Germany and the UK.

The traditional autumn air cargo tariff rate increases have been limited this year. Some airlines have raised rates on some routes, for instance to Asia, especially Japan and Korea or to Latin America but there has been no overall generalised increase, industry sources said.

Airlines have been keen to concentrate on rebuilding yields and maintain existing customer relationships, rather than simply push up prices because there has been a short term demand recovery, they added.

But fuel prices which have risen by more than 20 percent since June 1996 could result in higher air cargo costs, possibly in the form of a surcharge, rather than await spring next year, when the next formal rate changes are due to take place, the sources said.
